Geordie is the accent and dialect of Newcastle upon Tyne and Northeast England, marked by distinctive vowel pronunciations, rhotic speech, and strong working-class and regional identity. It preserves many historical features of Northern English and remains one of Britain's most distinctive and recognizable regional accents.

Geordie speakers use rhotic pronunciation of the r throughout, even word-finally and before consonants, as in Scottish English. There are distinctive vowel shifts as well. The strut vowel is pronounced more toward o, making "bus" sound like "bos," and "face" shifts toward the trap area. The consonants show interesting patterns too. The th sound sometimes becomes d at the start of words, so "that" becomes "dat." The soft g drops in -ing endings, so "running" becomes "runnin'."

Geordie uses the word "gan" for "go" and has distinctive grammatical forms like "yee" for "you" in the plural. The intonation patterns include characteristic rising and falling movements distinct from RP and other accents.

Strong local identity and cultural pride are central to Geordie. The accent has become more acceptable and even fashionable in contemporary British media. Geordie is another strongly rhotic Northern accent, similar to Scottish English in its regional pride and non-standard grammar. Like Scouse, the Liverpool accent, it is regionally distinctive and Northern-based. It has historically been marginalized against the prestige Southern standard of Received Pronunciation.
